## The problem

`scripts/lint-as-committed.mjs` extracts an isolated, committed copy of the repo tree
(`git clone --local --shared --no-checkout` + `checkout --detach <sha>`) to run a lint
against exactly the committed detector over exactly the committed content — never the
working tree, which may hold uncommitted or peer edits.

That extraction technique never recurses into git **submodules**. A checkout of a
commit that has a submodule (a `160000` gitlink tree entry) creates an **empty
directory** at the submodule's path — the gitlink metadata is present, the submodule's
own tree/blobs are not. So a lint (or typecheck) that resolves an import through a
submodule path (e.g. `libs/papercusp/libs/db/src/connection` in this repo) sees
nothing there and fabricates a spurious `TS2307`/module-not-found error the committed
code does not actually have. This was EI-21033860565861795.

## The obvious fix doesn't work

The natural fix looks like: point `submodule.<name>.url` at the caller's OWN local,
already-checked-out copy of the submodule (`repoRoot/<path>`), then run
`git submodule init && git submodule update` — cheap (a local-path clone
auto-hardlinks), no network, no credentials needed.

It fails anyway:

```
fatal: transport 'file' not allowed
fatal: clone of '/repo/libs/generic/memory' into submodule path '/tmp/.../libs/generic/memory' failed
```

This is git's post-CVE-2022-39253 hardening: `git submodule` commands refuse a
`file://`-style (including a bare local filesystem path) transport for a submodule
URL **by default**, specifically to stop a malicious commit's `.gitmodules` from
making git silently clone an attacker-chosen local path when a victim runs `git
submodule update` against an untrusted checkout. The restriction fires **even when
the URL was constructed by the caller's own script**, not read from the untrusted
`.gitmodules` — `git submodule` cannot distinguish "I set this URL myself, it's safe"
from "the untrusted commit set this URL". Overriding it globally
(`git config --global protocol.file.allow always`) would work, but reintroduces
exactly the class of vulnerability the hardening exists to close, for every future
`git submodule` invocation on the box — not an acceptable trade for one tool.

A plain **top-level** `git clone <local-path> <dest>` (not through the submodule
subsystem) is NOT subject to this restriction — that's ordinary, always-allowed local
clone behaviour. Nothing about "isolated-tree extraction" requires going through `git
submodule` machinery at all.

## The fix

Skip `git submodule` entirely. Treat each submodule as a second, independent
repository and clone it the same way the superproject itself was cloned:

1. Parse the checked-out tree's `.gitmodules` for `{ name, path, url }` (a submodule's
   config `name` can differ from its directory `path` — e.g. this repo's
   `[submodule "libs/git-graph"]` lives at `libs/generic/git-graph`).
2. For each submodule path, resolve the superproject's pinned commit:
   `git rev-parse <sha>:<path>` — a gitlink tree entry resolves to the commit sha it
   points at, the same way a blob entry resolves to its content sha. (You cannot
   resolve a file *inside* the submodule this way — `<sha>:<path-in-submodule>` from
   the superproject repo fails with `fatal: path '...' exists on disk, but not in
   'HEAD'`, because git does not recurse a pathspec across a submodule boundary. Read
   the submodule's OWN content with `git -C <submodule-repo> show <pin>:<rel-path>`.)
3. `git clone --local --shared --no-checkout --quiet <repoRoot>/<path> <workRoot>/<path>`
   — cloning into the ALREADY-EXISTING empty placeholder directory the earlier
   superproject checkout created; git permits cloning into an existing directory as
   long as it's empty.
4. `git -C <workRoot>/<path> checkout --detach --quiet <pin>`.

Do this **before** anything symlinks into the submodule's directory (e.g. a
`node_modules` link, if the submodule is itself an npm workspace) — `git clone`
refuses a non-empty target.

Fail closed if a submodule's local source (`repoRoot/<path>/.git`) doesn't exist:
this technique deliberately never fetches over the network (no credentials in an
isolated CI/agent context; a network attempt could hang on an SSH prompt). For the
default `--ref=HEAD`, the pinned commit is always resolvable locally (it's literally
what's checked out); for another ref it's reachable through the local checkout's own
fetched history, since these are full clones, not shallow ones.

## When this generalizes

Any tool that materializes an isolated copy of a committed tree via `git clone
--no-checkout` + `checkout --detach` (rather than a real `git checkout` in a live
working directory) will hit this if the repo has submodules — extraction and
submodule population are two separate concerns, and only the second one collides with
the file-transport hardening. If you're building a similar "run X against the exact
committed bytes" tool, budget for this from the start rather than discovering it via a
silently-wrong lint verdict.
